title: Fair Pacing: Client vs Server Admission - Mini lab sketch
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact working sketch of a micro-lab comparing two simple pacing/admission approaches to improve latency/cost fairness across tenants during microbursts: (A) client-driven pacing (clients back off and spread requests) vs (B) server-side admission (centralized token-bucket + priority policy). Focus: conversational chat-style traffic with short bursts and mixed-priority tenants.

Why this is different from other benches: many notes we have focus on batching, tiling, or prefetch tradeoffs. This one looks specifically at end-to-end fairness when burst arrivals are correlated across many tenants and the goal is to reduce p95 penalty for premium tiers without exploding unit cost for the platform. We intentionally keep models and hardware constant to isolate admission behavior.

Experiment setup (quick):
- Model: open-llm-xxl (dense FP16 baseline) with 1.6k context, decode length 64 avg.
- Hardware: dedicated 8xA100 pool (single region), fixed serving runtime config.
- Tenants: 30 simulated tenants, mix = {5 premium (SLA p95 < 300ms), 10 standard, 15 best-effort}.
- Baseline traffic: poisson arrivals per-tenant tuned to 0.6 steady concurrency (sustained).
- Burst injection: 30s microburst where all tenants raise rate x6 over baseline.
- Duration: 20 min per run, repeated 12 times for statistics.
- Metrics collected: p50, p90, p95 latency (end-to-end), tokenized cost-per-1k (approx unit cost proxy), slot utilization, dropped or delayed requests.

Two admission policies:
A) Client-driven pacing (CDP): we simulate a guidance API where server returns a dynamic pacing window to clients based on recent slot backlog. Clients space requests to respect window. No centralized queuing; best-effort fairness via per-client rate hints. Low implementation complexity for hosted API.

B) Server-side admission (SSA): centralized token-bucket with weighted priority. Premium tenants have higher token weight; if bucket exhausted, requests are delayed server-side until tokens refill. The admission enforces hard concurrency cap allowing fast failover to cheaper model variants for overflow (not used in this micro-lab).

Workload shape notes:
- Conversational patterns: many short turns (5-15 tokens in input), decode-heavy but short outputs.
- Burst shape: rise time ~2s, sustain 30s, decay ~5s (triangular-ish).

Results (aggregated medians across runs) - key rows only:
- Baseline (no pacing/admission):
  Premium p95: 980ms, Standard p95: 1150ms, Best-effort p95: 1400ms, Platform $/1k tokens (relative): 1.00
- CDP (client-driven):
  Premium p95: 420ms, Standard p95: 640ms, Best-effort p95: 1120ms, Platform $/1k tokens: 1.05
- SSA (server-side):
  Premium p95: 260ms, Standard p95: 590ms, Best-effort p95: 1300ms, Platform $/1k tokens: 1.12

Interpretation (rough):
- Both approaches reduce premium p95 substantially versus baseline; SSA gives the strongest premium latency improvement but at higher system cost (more delayed requests and slightly higher replays).
- CDP is cheaper and avoids central coordination but provides weaker protection for premium tenants vs SSA; however CDP retains lower tail for best-effort compared to SSA in our runs.
- SSA concentrates benefit to premium profile at the expense of best-effort; CDP spreads pain more evenly.

ASCII micro-chart (p95 by tenant class normalized to baseline=1.0):
  baseline | premium:1.00 --- standard:1.00 --- best-effort:1.00
  CDP      | premium:0.43 --- standard:0.56 --- best-effort:0.80
  SSA      | premium:0.27 --- standard:0.51 --- best-effort:0.93

Cost vs premium p95 tradeoff (rounded):
  Policy | platform $/1k | premium p95 (ms)
  -------+--------------+----------------
  baseline | 1.00       | 980
  CDP      | 1.05       | 420
  SSA      | 1.12       | 260

Operational notes and implementation risk:
- CDP relies on client compliance; mobile or third-party clients may misbehave, reducing effectiveness. Requires lightweight guidance API and client SDK changes.
- SSA requires server queuing and throttling primitives; simpler to enforce but increases server-side complexity and risk of head-of-line blocking if not per-tenant queueing.
- Both approaches interact with KV-caching and batching: admission delays can increase cache hit rates (good) but may also reduce batching efficiency if spacing removes natural concurrency. Need coupling tests.

Open questions / follow-ups:
1) How do policies interact with dynamic batching strategies (smallbatch vs dynbatch) and decode preemption?
2) What is the impact on observed tokenization cost if we enable immediate fallback to a smaller quantized model for overflow? (preliminary thought: SSA pairs well with fallbacks, CDP less so)
3) How tolerant are clients to pacing hints in real-world SDKs? Run field A/B on Canary customers.
4) Explore hybrid: server issues soft admission + client hints to reduce worst-case HO blocking.

Next immediate experiments (short to-dos):
- Run same micro-lab with 2 model variants (baseline and quant-compact fallback) and SSA enabling fallback at 80% capacity. (owner: Ethan)
- Replay with mobile client compliance noise (simulate 20% non-compliant clients) to see CDP fragility. (owner: Lina)
- Instrument slotization and batching metrics to measure whether admission increases or decreases packing efficiency (owner: Marcus)

Notes to reviewer:
- This is an early sketch intended for prioritization discussion with product and platform. Not production-ready; experimental harness and traffic generator code lives in linked PR above.
- If we like SSA, we should prototype a lightweight per-tenant leaky-bucket admission in the runtime (low risk) + a simple admin UI to tune weights. If we prefer CDP, invest in client SDK guidance primitives and a discovery endpoint.

Attachments (quick):
- small CSV excerpts attached in PR: runs-summary.csv (linked in PR), raw traces: s3://redwood-labs/fair-pacing/20261117/

Unresolved: pricing and customer communication if we adopt strict SSA (some best-effort tenants will get elevated tail; upstream billing/product needs to decide how to surface).

End of mini-lab sketch.

-- Priya
